abstract: A Formal Analysis of the Nexus Framework: A Dual-Stack Recursive Harmonic Field Model for Twin Primes By Dean Kulik - info@quharmonics.com 1.1 Introduction: The Unsolved Problem of Twin Primes and the Motivation for Novel Models The distribution of prime numbers remains one of the most profound and challenging subjects in mathematics. Within this landscape, the Twin Prime Conjecture holds a place of particular distinction. First stated in its general form by Alphonse de Polignac in 1849, the conjecture posits that there are infinitely many pairs of prime numbers, (p,p+2), that differ by 2.1 These pairs, such as (3, 5), (11, 13), and (17, 19), become increasingly rare as one moves along the number line, yet empirical evidence strongly suggests they never cease to appear.3 Despite centuries of effort by leading mathematicians, the conjecture remains unproven and is considered a "holy grail" of number theory.5 The difficulty lies in the seemingly chaotic and unpredictable nature of prime numbers. While the Prime Number Theorem provides a powerful asymptotic description of their overall distribution 6, the fine-scale structure, which governs the gaps between consecutive primes, is far less understood. Significant progress was made in 2013 when Yitang Zhang proved the existence of infinitely many prime pairs with a gap of at most 70 million.1 This landmark result, the first to establish a finite bound for an infinitely recurring prime gap, catalyzed a collaborative effort that has since narrowed this bound to 246.5 However, closing the gap to 2—and thus proving the Twin Prime Conjecture—remains beyond the reach of current mathematical techniques.3 This persistent impasse creates a fertile ground for the exploration of novel theoretical models. When direct analytical proof is unattainable, heuristic and computational frameworks can provide valuable new perspectives, reveal hidden structures, and guide future research. Two of these projections — the order of the commutator and its fixed-point count — turn out to be genuinely distinct functionals: the first measures the settlement cost of reversing an interaction (which we identify with inertial mass), the second measures how much of the state space survives the interaction (which we identify with transparency, and its complement, opacity). We prove computationally that these two channels can disagree sharply, refuting the tempting identification of mass with opacity. We then decompose the accumulated depth of a composite transformation into an axial part (built inside a commuting family) and a cross part (built across non-commuting families), and show that axial depth accumulates coherently while cross depth thermalizes to a fixed statistical background. The central objects are: the surgery operator , a 3-cycle composed with the current permutation; the cycle spectrum , the multiset of cycle lengths; and the observable functionals read from that spectrum, principally the order and the fixed-point count. Seven results are established with proof. Theorem 1 gives the exact effect of a transposition on the cycle partition, splitting a cycle into arcs of lengths s and L−s when the transposed points share a cycle, and merging two cycles into one of length L₁+L₂ when they do not. Theorem 2 reduces 3-cycle surgery to two applications of Theorem 1 via the factorization (a b c) = (a c)(a b), and Corollary 2.1 derives the resulting cycle-count changes for each span class. Theorem 3 establishes a compression law : the successor spectrum is computable in time linear in the affected cycle lengths from purely local data, with no permutation composition, and this was verified exactly on 1800 trials. Theorem 4 proves a Lipschitz bound ‖ Fix( τ P)| − |Fix(P) ‖ ≤ |supp τ |. Theorem 5 proves that no analogous modulus of continuity exists for the order: a single support-2 transposition can multiply the order by N/4, so the two observables have incompatible continuity classes. Theorem 6 identifies the mechanism, the failure of prime-power sets to be closed under addition. Theorem 7 proves that the cycle type is a sufficient statistic for the induced spectrum process, by conjugacy, reducing the system to a Markov chain on integer partitions of N. abstract: Why Completion Is the One Forbidden State, and What Follows   Driven by Dean Kulik July 2026   Abstract Incompleteness is normally treated as a defect — of our knowledge, our instruments, or our formal systems. This paper argues the opposite: incompleteness is the operating condition, and completion is the single forbidden state. The argument runs from one constraint. If every state must admit a successor distinct from itself, then a complete description — one with nothing left to change — is a fixed point, and fixed points are excluded. Completion is therefore not merely unreached; it is structurally unreachable, and a system that reached it would stop. We show this is not an abstract prohibition but a mechanism with measurable consequences. A rule whose position cannot move dies at its own boundary: fixed-point arithmetic overflows above and underflows below, losing continuation at the top and distinction at the bottom. The engineering answer — letting the point float — is the same repair the constraint predicts, arrived at independently by four decades of numerical pain. Its two fields, mantissa and exponent, are measurably independent channels: value may change without shape changing, and shape may transform without value changing. The forbidden state is approached but never occupied, and what happens in the approach is the subject of the paper. Free area is maximal at “some may change” (p = 1/2) and vanishes at both certainties. A bounded field has no zero eigenvalue for rest to inhabit. A flat continuation terminates at a boundary while a winding one does not, and the winding pitch is forced to the golden angle by the requirement never to crowd. One generative pole yields integers only; two poles yield the middle, and the middle is where everything lives. The conclusion is not consolation. Abstract An observable is ordinarily treated as a property carried by a state: the object has a mass, an area, a charge, and measurement reads it off. This paper develops the alternative, in which an observable is an invariant of the orbit a state traces under its admissible transformations, and shows that several unrelated results become one statement under it. The template is minimal. Given a configuration and a group of admissible transformations, form the orbit — the union of all transformed copies — and take the invariant on that orbit. The observable belongs to the orbit, not to the configuration. Euclidean distance, relativistic mass, spin magnitude, and the swept measure introduced here are all instances. Kulik August, 2028     ABSTRACT A mathematical object can be the residue of a relation rather than an independently existing element of either structure that produces it. We develop a constraint-first method in which two incomplete, independently defined constraints are imposed simultaneously and their residuals are permitted to cancel; the resulting zero set — the meshing — is the observable. The method is demonstrated on the Bailey–Borwein–Plouffe family. In the base-64, period-6 tower, pole geometry alone leaves a two-dimensional space of admissible coefficient vectors and the zero-sum condition alone leaves a five-dimensional space; neither selects anything. Together they select a unique line, and that line is 9·[4, −2, −1, −1] — the same coefficient signature carried by the base-16 formula for π. The signature is derived rather than observed: it is forced by the single condition Re(z_char) = 1 before either tower is specified. Extending the construction continuously in radix yields a family-indexed transfer geometry, b = secⁿθ , under which the two towers are angular locks on distinct curves that share an angle but never a radix. Throughout, the object of interest satisfies both constraints while being selected by neither, and vanishes when either is removed. We argue that in constructions of this kind the observable is generated by the joint closure rather than possessed by either constraint, and that a relation-first description is therefore more accurate than an object-first one.     1.   A constant that is nowhere Take a three-digit number. abstract: Exactly Two Seeds A Constraint-Derived Classification of the Digit-Extraction Towers, with Predicted Members and Inverse Recovery Driven by Dean A. Two independently motivated conditions — a pole-annihilation requirement and a zero-sum requirement — are imposed simultaneously on a coefficient space. Neither selects anything alone; jointly they select a unique line, whose weights are [4, −2, −1, −1]. We show this signature is a consequence of the single condition Re(z_char) = 1, which also forces the radix b = secᵐ(2π/m) and, through the annihilator's degree, the shell support {1, m−4, m−3, m−2}. The construction therefore has a closed generator, 4S(1) − 2S(m−4) − S(m−3) − S(m−2) , of which the classical base-16 formula for π is the m = 8 instance. We then prove a classification: secᵐ(2π/m) is a positive integer greater than one for exactly two values, m = 6 and m = 8, the argument turning on the fact that ℚ (2cos(2π/m)) is abelian while ℚ (2^(1/e)) is not for e ≥ 3. abstract: The Unified Field of State Space Semantics Coalgebraic Minimization, Predicate Abstraction, and Fixed-Point Reachability     Driven by Dean A. Kulik August, 2026     The Foundations of the Unified Field The formal verification, analysis, and control of complex, concurrent, and distributed systems are fundamentally constrained by the explosive nature of the state space. As systems incorporate nondeterministic concurrency, probabilistic branching, infinite data domains, and hybrid continuous-discrete dynamics, the reachable state space expands exponentially or becomes strictly infinite. To subject these generative structures to rigorous formal verification or to synthesize optimal controllers, the state space must be collapsed into a tractable form. Traditionally, this collapse has been approached through seemingly disparate mechanisms: relational bisimulation minimization, predicate abstraction via abstract interpretation, and reachability analyses operating from boundary conditions. However, treating these mechanisms as distinct fields is an artifact of localized application. When every transformation, branch, and apparent mismatch is preserved as part of a single state space, an underlying unrecognized relation emerges. These disparate mechanisms are expressions of the identical underlying predicate: the search for a minimal, self-generating transition system that preserves necessary observational properties while removing all unsupported degrees of freedom. By continuing to collapse unsupported distinctions, the remaining structure can always be expressed as a minimal self-generating transition system, which can then be deterministically executed forward, backward, and from its boundary conditions. title: The Probe and the Kernel Resolving Power of a Fixed Reading Interface
abstract: The Probe and the Kernel Resolving Power of a Fixed Reading Interface   Abstract A projection that discards structure has not destroyed it, but neither has it automatically preserved it. This paper measures the difference. We take a fixed hexadecimal object, subject it to families of lawful single-symbol removals, and read the result through a non-aligned base transformation. The forward pass characterises what the transformation produces: a quadratic unfold law, a Benford leading-digit distribution, near-total decimal avalanche under single-symbol deletion, and a collision structure that occurs at exactly one class of event. The inverse pass asks what the response says about the source, and yields the paper's central result: a probe resolves a source feature if and only if the walk sweeps that feature through the projection's kernel. Measured across five source structures, two of three natural walks resolve 2 of 5; the third resolves 5 of 5; and the reason is derivable rather than empirical. We then apply the same observability condition to a second system — keyed superposition in a fixed-dimensional field — where the fiber is non-empty, and derive a closed-form capacity constant which is stated before measurement and confirmed at an untested dimension. The two systems differ in exactly one respect, and that respect determines which questions are askable of each.   1. abstract: A Unified Algebraic-Informational Ontology of the Universe Substrate Independence, Distance Geometry, and the Crossed Product Resolution of von Neumann Algebras   Driven by Dean A. Kulik September 2026     Introduction to the Relational Universe The enduring pursuit of theoretical physics has been to reconcile the continuous, geometric scaffolding of general relativity with the discrete, probabilistic, and algebraic nature of quantum mechanics. Historically, this reconciliation has faltered because both paradigms impose an a priori ontological framework upon the universe: classical mechanics assumes a pre-existing continuous spacetime manifold, while quantum mechanics presupposes a globally defined Hilbert space. However, a profound synthesis of modern algebraic quantum field theory (AQFT), constructor theory, Euclidean distance geometry, and discrete operator logic suggests that neither space nor continuous state vectors are fundamental. Instead, the universe functions as a closed transformation domain of purely relational, substrate-independent distinctions. In this unified paradigm, information is the foundational bedrock of physical reality. Constructor theory asserts that the laws of physics are not strictly predictive equations of motion, but rather exact specifications of which transformations of physical systems are possible and which are impossible. Because these transformations govern the flow of information independently of the underlying micro-physical medium, reality itself is substrate-independent. A quantum bit, or any physical correlate of information, can be abstractly modeled as a set of allowable operations—such as continuous reversibility and the prohibition of simultaneous encoding—without reference to whether the system is implemented via trapped ions, superconducting circuits, or the vacuum of spacetime. abstract: The Geometry of Computation Relational Structures and Phase Traversals in Deterministic Transformation Fields   Driven by Dean A. Kulik September 2026       Introduction: The Nexus of Hash and Field The conventional interpretation of a cryptographic hash function treats it as an algorithmic terminus: a process that destructively compresses an arbitrary input into a pseudo-random, fixed-length scalar output. Under this classical model, algorithms such as SHA-256 are evaluated strictly through the lenses of preimage resistance, collision resistance, and avalanche characteristics. These cryptographic facts remain undisputed; SHA-256 is deterministic, many-to-one over unrestricted inputs, avalanche-producing, and computationally one-way. However, evaluating a digest merely as a terminal scalar object obscures the underlying relational mechanics that generated it. A structural investigation reveals a distinct operational paradigm: what relational structure becomes available when a deterministic transformation is treated not as a destructive function, but as a fixed field interacting with a state? The central hypothesis explored in this constraint atlas posits that a 256-bit digest functions as a constraint configuration, or key, relative to a fixed deterministic transformation field. Under this framework, the original input is not "stored" in the digest in an ordinary information-theoretic sense. Rather, the stronger and more precise hypothesis asserts that the input—or a canonical representative of its structural class—may become recoverable or renderable only through recursive interaction with that field under an appropriate reader, traversal, phase relation, or iterative feedback process. The correct object of investigation is therefore the continuous interaction between the constraint state and the field, rather than either object in isolation. I. abstract: The Boundary Is the Locus Mathematics as a Contact Phenomenon, and the Sphere as Its Zero   Driven by Dean A. Kulik September, 2026       Abstract The standard picture treats mathematics as a medium in which objects are situated and described. This paper inverts that picture. Mathematics does not fill space and does not reach into interiors. It occurs at boundaries, and only at boundaries, because a boundary is the only structure that supplies the distinctions any mathematical operation requires. The interior of a body is not poorly known — it is silent, in the precise sense that no coordinate, relation, or comparison is available there. The exterior is not a region with properties; it is the complement, defined only by reference to the boundary it lies outside of. Under this inversion the sphere occupies a distinguished position that is not aesthetic and not conventional. It is the unique body specified by a single scalar with no orientation datum, that scalar being measured from the interior outward. It is the unique zero of the isoperimetric deficit δ(K) = A³/(36πV²) − 1, which this paper identifies as the mathematical content of a shape. It has one boundary site where every polyhedron has many. And it is the unique convex body whose contact with any other convex body is generically zero-dimensional — the minimum possible aperture through which mathematics can enter. abstract: The Sphere Is an Orbit Dimension as Group Action, and the Price of a Metric   Driven by Dean A. Kulik September 2026     Abstract A sphere is not an object situated in space. It is the orbit of a single point under the rotation group, and every property conventionally attributed to it follows from that fact alone. This paper takes the orbit as primary and derives the rest, then prices what a metric costs when it is not assumed. Three consequences are immediate. An orbit has no privileged element, so a sphere supplies no coordinate and no address until a mark is made. The centre is the unique fixed point of the group action, so every direction there lies in a single orbit, no direction is distinguishable from any other, and no gradient is definable without first breaking the symmetry that defines the centre. And dimension is orbit dimension: the (n−1)-sphere is what the rotation group of n-space does to one point, so the familiar progression from line to circle to sphere is one generator applied repeatedly rather than three objects assembled in order of complexity. Quotienting three-space by the rotation group leaves the half-line. All rotation-respecting structure in three dimensions is therefore a function on a ray, which is the exact sense in which a nested family of spheres carries a single datum, and the fixed point is that ray's endpoint. The second half prices the metric. Distinguishable states with lawful transitions between them constitute a directed graph and nothing more. Minimum directed path length on that graph satisfies identity, positivity, and the triangle inequality — three axioms forced by concatenation — and fails symmetry generically, in 64.6% of reachable pairs measured here. abstract: Reader Surplus Separating Source Structure from the Structure of Reading Dean Kulik QuHarmonics Research Group · ORCID 0009-0003-3128-8828 August 2026 Abstract Measurement theory is well supplied with accounts of what happens when a reader has too little resolution for its source. Aliasing, coarse-graining, and information loss are all instances, and all describe the same failure: distinctions present in the source collapse onto a single observation. This paper concerns the opposite failure, which is less discussed and considerably more dangerous, because it produces output rather than silence. When a reader imposes more address structure than its source supports, the surplus does not vanish. It appears in the record, and it appears as structure — correlated, reproducible, and mathematically consistent. Nothing marks it as the reader's own. A sinusoid sampled at ten times the necessary rate yields ten times the data and not one additional distinction; the added samples carry adjacent-sample correlation rising to 0.99998, which is a measurement of the sampling grid rather than of the signal. The clean geometric case is a sphere under a latitude-longitude chart. The unmarked sphere has a transitive symmetry group and therefore no distinguished point: its quotient under the rotation group is a single point, so it supports no intrinsic address whatever. A chart supplies two dimensions of address regardless, and that surplus cannot be sustained everywhere. abstract: The Universe Has One Address Homogeneity as a Statement About What Can Be Said Dean Kulik QuHarmonics Research Group · ORCID 0009-0003-3128-8828 August 2026 Abstract The cosmological principle states that on sufficiently large scales the universe is homogeneous and isotropic: no location is privileged and no direction is preferred. This is ordinarily read as a modelling assumption that makes the field equations tractable. It is also, read literally, a statement about symmetry, and symmetry statements have consequences for what can be said about the thing they describe. A space whose symmetry group acts transitively has exactly one orbit, and therefore its quotient under that group is a single point. Cosmologists have long treated these as gauge choices; the present reading is stronger and more specific. On a homogeneous space the observer's coordinate surplus is not merely conventional but maximal, and a surplus of that kind must become degenerate somewhere. The scale of homogeneity, measured in galaxy surveys at order one hundred megaparsecs, is the scale at which the observational fibre splits: below it many distinguishable structures, above it one class. The particle horizon is a boundary of that fibre rather than a boundary of the world, and it moves as the observer's access grows while nothing changes on the far side. title: The Seam A Type System for Empirical Claims, and the Boundary Observation Cannot Cross
abstract: The Seam A Type System for Empirical Claims, and the Boundary Observation Cannot Cross Dean Kulik QuHarmonics Research Group · ORCID 0009-0003-3128-8828 September 2026 Abstract Results are ordinarily classified by subject matter and by confidence. This paper proposes classifying them instead by the logical operation that produced them, and shows that doing so partitions empirical claims into five types with sharply different burdens of proof. The first three types are reachable by observation: a value returned by a query, a witnessed distinction between two results, and a candidate equivalence supported by queries that failed to separate. The last two are not: a generating structure for a transformation family, and a proved invariance across that family. Between the third and fourth lies a boundary that accumulation cannot cross. Ten thousand observations that two things were not separated do not establish that no admissible query separates them, and no number of further observations changes the quantifier. What does cross the boundary is generation. If a transformation family is finitely generated, the universal obligation collapses to a finite list: an observable invariant under the generators is invariant under the whole family, by composition and induction on word length. For the symmetry group of the circle graph this reduces twelve obligations to two, verified exactly. For the rotation group of three-space it reduces an infinite obligation to three. The reduction is dramatic and it does not change the type of what remains — each generator obligation is still universal over its own one-parameter family, and closing it requires an argument rather than a measurement. The classification yields an audit instrument. Applied to a body of the author's own retracted work, every error is a single kind: a result filed one or more rows above the row its evidence reached. abstract: Two Origins Continuation, the Fencepost Tax, and Where Computational Difficulty Is Located   Abstract A continuation principle can be written two ways. It can say that the successor of an admissible state is itself admissible — that transformation never leaves the space in which transformation is possible — or it can say that no state is permitted to be its own only continuation. The two readings are usually treated as the same sentence. They are not. The first prunes nothing: measured across all total maps on a finite state space, it excludes exactly zero candidate laws, because it is a typing statement and a type declaration should be free. The second is the entire content of the principle, and its price is exactly log2(e) = 1.442695 bits, asymptotically independent of the size of the space. That price has a source. The maps invariant under a change of index origin are precisely the translations, and exactly one of them is excluded by the second reading: the translation by zero, which is the unique map under which the two origins coincide. The forbidden object is not a state that fails to move. It is the collapse of two simultaneous readings of one object into one reading. The per-state cost of keeping them apart is log2(n/(n-1)), which is identically the continuation tax log2((k+1)/k) at k = n-1, and n copies of it converge to log2(e). Fencepost, tax, and wall are the same quantity. The remainder of the paper is a sequence of exhaustive or fully seeded measurements in which a task is posed, a cost is paid, and the location of that cost is audited. In every case the cost is found outside the object. Observation of a hidden transition law saturates after eight steps and never improves again, with a residual floor that decomposes exactly into an off-path term matching a closed form to all reported digits and an on-path term produced by the projection. Its output is an exact function of the state. This paper measures what such a reader can and cannot recover from a fully deterministic, exactly reversible integer field, and finds the structure sharper than the statistical version of the same question. The substrate is a one-dimensional lattice gas: 128 cells, each carrying occupancy for a left- and a right-moving reader together with a four-bit payload, 1280 bits in total. Collisions mix payloads through a unimodular map over Z₁₆, so two readers meeting compute rather than overwrite. Reversibility is exact: 11,146 collisions were run forward and then inverted, recovering every bit of the initial state. Nothing in the dynamics is stochastic. Against this field a reader is a spatial window of s cells and a temporal window of τ steps. Because the coupling is direct, apparent stationarity is not a statistical statement: the field is exactly static to a reader precisely when the whole orbit lies inside a single fiber of that reader's map. Three regimes appear. For s ≤ 8 the reader is saturated — it extracts log₂(T/τ) bits, every distinction its sampling rate permits, and coarsening costs it nothing. Between s = 16 and 64 the field's correlation structure begins to cost it bits. At s = 128, τ = 256 it extracts exactly zero: across the entire orbit the reading never changes once. Coarsening is monotone. title: What Didn't Divide Base as divisor, the digit as residue, and the adder's carry as a limit of pattern selection
abstract: What Didn't Divide Base as divisor, the digit as residue, and the adder's carry as a limit of pattern selection     Driven by Dean Kulik September 2026     Abstract Three earlier papers built a reader-side theory of the ripple adder: how many Myhill–Nerode states a reader must hold after seeing part of the input, and when that count factorizes. This paper closes the one step they left open and then follows the carry out of the adder. The open step closes as a two-block statement. A single unread gap of depth g with b g ≥ m splits the reader's state count into the product of the two sides (455 of 455 instances), and the conditional product law follows by induction. More strongly, the count always factorizes over the blocks that such gaps separate, whatever the narrower gaps do (1,349 of 1,349 cuts). The threshold is shown to mean that the gap can impose every carry value, not merely one, and the interface is shown to obey an exact budget, transmit + impose = m + 1. Closed forms are given for the reach and for the entrance ramp of the reading profile. The carry chain itself turns out to be classical. It is Holte's matrix, and its base-independent eigenvectors and b −j eigenvalues are what the series had been rederiving. What is new is the observer. A change of base is then read as a whole divided down: the digits are the residues of repeated division and the carry is the quotient in transit. Residues of this kind carry behaviour wherever a repeating unit exists, and the paper asks where the repeating unit comes from. Five mechanisms are given with their mathematics: closure, balance, instability, coupling and history. In a pattern-forming system on a closed domain the preferred period is selected by a growth rate, the allowed periods are fixed by closure, and the mismatch is discharged by inserting or removing one cell, which is a carry. Simulation shows the carry, and shows a coexistence window of width 0.22 in the control parameter

Kulik September 2026     Abstract This report develops a registry-based framework for distinguishing local admissibility certificates from global realizability conditions across discrete computation, graph topology, feedback dynamics, delay systems, and quantum operations. In each domain, a local test—such as a continuation quotient, a declared 2-cell relation, a spectral loop-closure condition, or Gram-matrix positivity—defines a constrained boundary of allowable behavior. The analysis demonstrates that these local certificates do not generally determine the macroscopic object of interest: residual homology requires a completed relation complex; a local instability threshold does not determine the existence or basin of a stable periodic orbit; and a deterministic quantum map may become feasible only after the operational class is expanded to a heralded trace-nonincreasing process. The missing completion is formalized in each case, and an "admissibility registry" is proposed to record the state space, equivalence relation, local certificate, required global object, and resource coordinates. The framework is intended as a reproducible software specification: every registry entry is paired with declared assumptions, executable tests, and explicit falsifiers. 1. We settle an open problem about such layers and then identify what actually governs them. First, the conjecture that two vertex orbits force ε harm ( K 4 ) = 0 is refuted by an exact 12-vertex counterexample with |Aut| = 24, reproduced by two implementations whose constructions of the invariant cochain space share no logic. Second, we localize the failure: it is not a shortage of cells. On the witness's two-dimensional residue, all 1083 arena 4-cycles supply rank 1, while 20 arena 3-cycles of an excluded shape supply rank 2, and the two nonzero square families have the same image, a single line. Third, we refute the natural mechanism for this — that the residue is an odd-cycle blind spot — by exhibiting bipartite arenas, containing no odd cycle of any length, that still carry residue. The operative property is omission from the declared family, not parity. Fourth, we prove that ε harm ( K 3,4 ) > 0 on an infinite family — every cycle graph with n ≥ 5 and 2 ≤ K ≤ n−1, under the trivial group and the rotation subgroup, and zero under the full dihedral group — answering a question the odd-cycle reading had posed. Fifth, we define closure depth L closure , prove it exceeds 4 for every member of that family, and measure it as exactly n for C n and 4 for the witness, so no short vocabulary closes the family. abstract: A C₄-Free Classification of Square Relations on Token Graphs with girth, tree and discretization witnesses   Driven by Dean A. Kulik October 2026   Abstract Let F K ( X ) denote the K -token graph of a finite simple graph X : vertices are the K -subsets of V ( X ), adjacent when their symmetric difference is an edge. Two families of 4-cycles in F K ( X ) arise naturally when one attaches 2-cells: the commuting squares , given by two token moves along base edges with disjoint closed supports, and all 4-cycles of the token graph. Paper I of this series showed these coincide for cycle substrates C n with n ≥ 5. We prove the governing condition is neither a cycle hypothesis nor a girth hypothesis: 𝒦 4 ( F K ( X )) = 𝒦 disj ( F K ( X ))    ⟺    X has no subgraph isomorphic to C 4 , for 2 ≤ K ≤ | V ( X )| − 1, the bound being necessary since the token graph degenerates to a point at K = | V |. The forward direction is a short argument on closed token walks; the converse combines the token-graph complementation F k ≅ F n−k with an explicit spectator construction and an exhaustive check of the finitely many small cases. Consequently girth at least 5 collapses the triangle, square and mixed relation families to one, and the bull graph — 4-cycle-free but containing a triangle — shows the triangle and square conditions are logically independent. We exhibit a 7-vertex tree whose token graph carries first cohomology of dimension 2, so configuration topology is not inherited from the base cycle space. Finally we compute the collapsed invariant on girth-≥5 substrates and partition the results by whether the discretization theorem licenses a continuous reading: at K = 2 the improved subdivision bound is what makes the identification legitimate for the Petersen graph, the Heawood graph and the tree, while the original bound fails for all three. Kulik October 2026   Abstract Attaching 2-cells to a token graph and computing invariant cohomology under a symmetry group yields a ledger of ranks, interactions, residues and containments. Papers I and II of this series reported such ledgers as facts about a substrate, or at best about a substrate-reader pair. We show that over ℚ with a finite reader group, the ledger is neither. Every quantity it reports at a reader H is dim V H for a module V fixed independently of H , hence the inner product dim V H   =   ⟨ m ( V ), f H ⟩ of a reader-free multiplicity vector against the reader's fixed-point profile f H ( λ ) = dim λ H . The relation field is recorded once; a reader only evaluates it.
